Closing the Gap

What Hawaiʻi would raise by taxing capital gains at 9 percent, or at the same rates as wages, now that Act 24 has raised the top rate on work to 13 percent.

Hawaiʻi Appleseed · Model run September 23, 2026 · Tax years 2027 to 2031

$128 million
Tax gains as ordinary income. Revenue in tax year 2027, residents.
$47 million
Raise the cap to 9 percent. Revenue in tax year 2027, residents.
88 percent
Share of the ordinary-rates increase paid by the top 1 percent of households.
5.75 points
Gap between the top rate on wages and the rate on capital gains under Act 24.

The Gap Act 24 Widened

HAWAIʻI TAXES MOST INCOME on a graduated schedule, but long-term capital gains get a special ceiling. Under the alternative tax in state law, net capital gains are taxed at no more than 7.25 percent, however high the filer’s other income.1

Act 24 of 2026 added a 13 percent bracket above $1 million of taxable income for joint filers ($750,000 for heads of household, $500,000 for single filers) and raised the rates between $350,000 and $1 million.2 It left the capital gains ceiling where it was. The distance between the top rate on wages and the rate on capital gains therefore grew from 3.75 points to 5.75 points.

That matters for what closing the gap would raise. Taxing gains at ordinary rates now brings gains up to 13 percent rather than 11 percent, so the same option is worth more under Act 24 than it was under the Act 46 brackets it replaced. Figure 1 compares the two. A 9 percent cap is nearly unchanged, because it does not depend on the ordinary rates.

Under Act 24, taxing capital gains as ordinary income would raise about $40 million more in tax year 2027 than the same change would have under the Act 46 brackets.

What Each Option Would Raise

TAXING CAPITAL GAINS AS ORDINARY INCOME would raise an estimated $128 million from Hawaiʻi residents in tax year 2027, the first year a bill passed in 2027 could reach. Raising the ceiling to 9 percent would raise about $47 million.

Both figures account for investors selling less when the tax on selling rises. The model reduces realized gains by 2 percent for each point the state rate goes up. Without that response, the estimates would be $170 million and $58 million. Figure 2 shows how revenue grows through 2031 as gains grow with the economy.4

How sure are these numbers? The biggest uncertainty is how gains split between filers just above and far above $1 million, since the top bracket applies only to the second group. State data puts about 80 percent of the gains in the top income class above $1 million. Moving that between 70 percent and the roughly 92 percent that national data implies gives a range of $119 million to $136 million for ordinary rates in 2027, and $47 million to $48 million for the 9 percent cap.

Who Would Pay

ALMOST ALL OF THE NEW REVENUE would come from the highest-income households, because that is where capital gains are. Under ordinary rates, the top 1 percent of households, those with income above about $703K, would pay 88 percent of the increase, an average of $25,547 each. The next 4 percent would pay 11 percent.

Households in the bottom 60 percent would pay nothing more under either option: their income is taxed at rates below the 7.25 percent ceiling, so the ceiling does not lower their tax today, and raising or repealing it changes nothing for them. Figure 3 shows each group’s share of the total, and Table 2 the average change per household.

Checking Against Earlier Estimates

IN NOVEMBER 2025, Hawaiʻi Appleseed published estimates from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy for the same two options, for tax year 2026 under the Act 46 brackets then in law: $44 million for a 9 percent cap and $85 million for ordinary rates.5

Scored on the same year and brackets, this model lands within a few million dollars of both once the realization response is included, as Table 3 shows. That agreement is the basis for trusting the Act 24 estimates above, which use the same method with the new brackets.

Gains Earned by Nonresidents

THE FIGURES ABOVE COUNT RESIDENTS ONLY, to match the earlier estimates. Nonresidents who sell Hawaiʻi property or hold interests in Hawaiʻi businesses also pay the alternative tax on those gains. In a typical year, the model estimates they would add about $29 million to the ordinary-rates option and $11 million to the 9 percent cap in tax year 2027.

Nonresident gains swing widely from year to year. At tax year 2022 levels, when nonresident gains spiked, the add-on would be $64 million and $24 million. Both figures include the realization response.6

How These Estimates Are Made

THE MODEL BUILDS a synthetic population of about 39,990 Hawaiʻi tax units from the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey microdata (HI 5yr 2020-24), calibrated to state tax data and projected forward with Congressional Budget Office growth rates. Filers with income above $1 million, whom survey data miss, are added from IRS and state tax statistics.

Capital gains are anchored to the Department of Taxation’s count of resident long-term gains eligible for the alternative rate, by income class, then grown each year.6 Tax is computed as the statute defines the alternative tax, not with the simple shortcut of taxing gains at the lower of the bracket rate and the ceiling. The realization response and the split of gains at the top are the two assumptions that move the estimates most, and both are stated above.

The full method, including every parameter, is documented in the source code.3
